evidence.excerpt: This book will help you find the weak part instead of blaming “AI” as though it were one indivisible object. Read the chapters in order to build the complete picture. Use the separate Concept Index when you need to look up one term—such as token, context, memory, routing or agent—and then jump to the chapter where that term does real work.

This is the first lesson of the whole book: the quality of an AI result depends on more than the wording of one prompt. It depends on what the system is trying to help you do, what information reached it, what operations ran, what the model produced and what you checked before acting.

Later chapters will open each part carefully: how models are trained and run; how tokens and context windows affect what fits; how session and memory differ; what retrieval, tools, permissions, routing and wrappers add; how agents and multi-step loops work; and why convincing answers can still fail. The Concept Index will let you find any one term without turning the book itself into a dictionary.

You did not consult one all-knowing thing. You used an **AI system**: the whole working arrangement that received your request and produced the result. That arrangement includes the product you opened, the instructions and material available for this task, at least one trained model, and the software that presents the answer. Some systems can also search, calculate, retrieve documents or take actions. The exact arrangement varies from product to product.

The **model** is an important part of that system, but it is not the whole system. It is the trained component that processes input and produces an output. The product and surrounding software shape what reaches it, which other capabilities are available and what you eventually see.
We will begin with one decision and follow it all the way through. Nothing floats around as a loose definition. Every part earns its name by changing what happens next.

Not every AI product has the same tools, and not every available tool runs on every request. The useful question is not “Does this AI have tools?” It is “What operation actually ran for this answer, and can I inspect what came back?”

1. **What decision am I actually trying to make?** If the system solved a narrower problem, restate the real one.
2. **What information did this answer actually use?** Check the messages, files, dates and missing facts that mattered.
3. **What current source or operation supports the consequential claims?** Inspect the returned evidence; do not treat fluency as a citation.

aiEditorialAnalysis.prompt: Why can't the Census finding that 30% of men versus 17% of women use AI daily be taken as evidence that women are less able or less interested in AI?
aiEditorialAnalysis.response: Because frequency of use reflects the conditions someone works under, not just her choices. If one worker is given an approved tool, paid time to practise and an invitation to evaluate a process, and another is simply told to keep up, the first will log more use regardless of relative ability or enthusiasm. The survey also only measured self-reported frequency among people who had already used AI for at least one task — it never asked about skill, interest, access, or whether daily use would even help each job. So the gap is compatible with unequal conditions and cannot identify a cause.
aiEditorialAnalysis.expectedEvidence: A correct answer must distinguish what was measured (self-reported frequency among prior users, March 2026) from what was not (ability, interest, access, usefulness), and cite the conditions mechanism: tool provision, paid learning time and invitations drive usage independently of aptitude.
aiEditorialAnalysis.assessment: The artifact fully supports this answer: P003 defines the measured population, P004 lists what the figures do not measure, and P006 supplies the causal conditions mechanism with its explicit limit.

aiEditorialAnalysis.prompt: Using the article's mechanism, what does the 3x usage gap show, and what is wrong with staffing the committee from the highest-volume users?
aiEditorialAnalysis.response: The usage gap measures conditions, not aptitude: day-shift nurses have supported access (IT help, scheduled training time), so higher volume tells us little about night nurses' ability or interest. Selecting the committee from existing heavy users repeats the P007 selection error — people who never had supported access lose the next opportunity too, so the gap compounds. The hospital should instead examine how it distributes training time and support across shifts, and open committee selection beyond current users; rising login counts alone would not show the decisions became fairer.
aiEditorialAnalysis.expectedEvidence: Application of two article moves: (1) frequency reflects access conditions, not ability (P004, P006); (2) selecting participants from existing users compounds the access gap, and usage metrics cannot verify fairness (P007).
aiEditorialAnalysis.assessment: The article's mechanism transfers cleanly to this unseen case: both the measurement critique and the compounding-selection step apply without modification, confirming the explanation generalizes.
